title: Bisect hypothesis journal & dashboard playbook
content:
Purpose
This is a lightweight, hypothesis-driven runbook for tracking performance regressions that require a bisect and dashboard correlation work. The goal is to make investigations reproducible, reduce noisy churn by focusing on prioritized hypotheses, and provide clear guardrails for canary comparisons and rollback thresholds.

When to use this doc
- Alerts that show step changes in tail latency (p95/p99) or throughput drops that persist beyond brief noise windows (>= 15 minutes).
- Canary shows divergence between baseline and candidate (traffic split) beyond configured delta for two consecutive evaluation windows.
- Regressions that are not solved by basic config toggles (batching, instance count) and need code-level bisect or profiling.

Quick triage checklist (5–15 min)
1) Check high-level dashboards: Serving runtime overview (dashboard: Serving Runtime - Overview), Per-model latency heatmap, gpu/cpu utilization summary.
2) Confirm scope: single model / all models / certain route / region. Note routes and model ids.
3) Look at traffic changes: request rate, seq length distribution, payload size.
4) Check recent deploys: list commits in last 24h; annotate timeline in the alert.
5) If scope != global and traffic is stable, proceed to hypothesis stage. If global and coincides with infra events, escalate to SRE.

Important dashboards & queries to run
- Grafana panels (names):
  - Serving Runtime - Overview (latency histograms, p50/p95/p99)
  - Model-level Latency Heatmap (split by model & route)
  - KV-cache hit rate and eviction counters
  - Batch size distribution (per-instance)
  - GPU utilization + memory pressure per node
  - Trace-sample comparison (baseline vs candidate)
- PromQL examples:
  - p99 latency (route): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(serving_latency_bucket{route=~"%ROUTE%"}[5m])) by (le))
  - average batch size: sum(rate(serving_batch_size_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(serving_batch_size_count[5m]))
  - KV cache hit rate: sum(rate(kv_cache_hits[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests[5m]))
- Tracing: compare span durations for these spans: "model.prepare_inputs", "model.forward", "runtime.kv_lookup", "runtime.batch_flush"

Hypothesis journal (structured, one hypothesis per row)
For each hypothesis, capture: id, short description, why plausible, metric to detect, acceptance criteria, quick test to run, owner, status. Use this journal to drive the bisect.
Example entries (fill during investigation):
- H1: "KV cache eviction spike caused p99 increase"
  - Why: eviction rate + memory pressure increased at same timestamp as latency spike
  - Metric: kv_cache_evictions, kv_cache_hit_rate, p99 latency for long-seq requests
  - Test: replay 10k requests with same seq distribution on baseline vs candidate; compare p99 and KV metrics
  - Acceptance: if candidate p99 > baseline p99 by > 15% and eviction rate higher, keep H1 as likely
  - Owner: Marcus
  - Status: in_progress

- H2: "Batching regression due to changed batching window/timing"
  - Why: batch size distribution moved towards smaller batches at the same time as deploy
  - Metric: average batch size, batch_wait_ms, p50/p95 latency for short vs long sequences
  - Test: force fixed batching policy (local flag) and measure latencies for both builds
  - Owner: Priya
  - Status: proposed

Bisect protocol (commit-based)
1) Preconditions: automated perf harness available (see linked_artifacts PR), deterministic-ish workloads for unit tests, synthetic replay tool: replay-load.py.
2) Define good and bad commit SHAs from deployment timeline. Ensure reproducible test harness with env: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, model weights pinned, quantization knobs identical.
3) Run binary search: check midpoint commit, run 3 iterations of the benchmark (light load + burst), collect p50/p95/p99, batch metrics, KV metrics. If results are noisy, increase iterations.
4) Stopping criteria: commit identified when midpoint result is significantly different vs baseline (two-sided t-test p < 0.01 on log-latencies or non-parametric KS test on latency distributions).
5) Post-bisect: open PR link to commit, annotate hypothesis journal with root cause hypothesis and evidence.

Canary comparison methodology
- Canary window: 10m evaluation windows x 6 windows for 1 hour. Require divergence in at least 4/6 windows for p95 or error rate.
- Metrics to compare: p95, p99, error rate, average tokens/sec per instance, batch size median.
- Statistical test: use KS test on latency distributions between baseline and canary for each window; also compute relative delta and check against configured threshold (default p95 delta 12%).
- Visualization: overlay CDFs of request latencies for baseline vs canary and a small table of batch metrics. Attach representative traces for slow tails.

Profiling commands (run on a repro node)
- Quick CPU sample (1 minute): sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60 && sudo perf report --stdio > perf-report.txt
- CUDA sampling (NVIDIA Nsight Systems): nsys profile -o nsys-repro.qdrep -t cuda,osrt -w true --trace=cuda,osrt --force-overwrite --sample=cpu-cycles <command>
- PyTorch profiler (when running model locally): python -m torch.profiler --schedule wait=1,warmup=1,active=3 --on_trace_ready=trace_handler <script>
- LLMTuner microbenchmark: run micro-benchmarks at multiple sequence lengths (8/64/512) and log kernel timings. Save raw traces for comparisons.

Reproduction harness & synthetic plan
- Use replay-load.py with a sealed dataset for the model/route; seed RNG for deterministic ordering. Payloads: short (<= 32 tokens), medium (128), long (>= 512). Weight by production distribution.
- Recommended profile matrix: small load (4 RPS), steady load (50 RPS), burst (200 RPS for 30s). Run each for baseline/candidate 3x. Collect histograms and traces.

Rollback and mitigation criteria
- Immediate rollback if: p99 increases > 30% with error rate increase > 0.5% and root cause unknown.
- Temporary mitigation: scale up instances + force older batching configuration or enable cached weights, if that reduces p99 by > 15% in canary testing, consider urgent patch.

Postmortem skeleton (to fill after resolution)
- Summary: what happened, timeline, impact area, customer-facing impact (if any)
- Root cause: evidence linking code change or infra event to regression
- Mitigations enacted: immediate mitigation + permanent fix planned
- Lessons learned: monitoring gaps, test coverage gaps, dashboard improvements required
- Follow-ups: owner + due date

Useful links & quick references
- Perf harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness (see /benchmarks/replay-load.py)
- Grafana dashboard (Serving Runtime - Overview): https://grafana.internal/d/84f2/serving-runtime-overview
- Example PR that added batching change: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/876
- Slack thread template: #eng-serving-runtime perf-incident-{YYYYMMDD} (post initial triage there)

Notes & heuristics (team memory)
- Watch sequence-length shifts closely; even moderate increases in long-seq proportion (5%->12%) can push p99 through KV cache miss storms.
- Small changes to batching timing (ms-level) can break kernel fusion opportunities on some GPUs; always test at multiple seq lengths.
- Kernel-level regressions often show up as high GPU SM utilization with rising stall cycles; pair Nsight runs with kernel timing diffs.

Owner for this doc: Ava Chen — update the hypothesis journal during active investigations and move resolved items to a postmortem.

Appendix: minimal reproducible command examples
- Run replay (example): python perf-harness/benchmarks/replay-load.py --model-id redwood/gpt-small --dataset data/replays/route-123.json --duration 300 --rps 50 --seed 42 --out-dir /tmp/perf-run
- Run bisect harness (example): ./bisect-run.sh --good <good_sha> --bad <bad_sha> --harness /tmp/perf-run --iterations 3 --metric p99

End of doc
